title: Org Pulse
tagline: 25 questions. 5 minutes. A precise read on where your organization is thriving — and where pressure is quietly building.
instructions: Answer based on your current reality — not how you wish things were.

_distinctness.clarity: Priorities, roles, and direction are clearly communicated and understood.
_distinctness.accountability: Commitments are kept; underperformance is named, not ignored.
_distinctness.talent: Right people in the right seats; retention is intentional, not accidental.
_distinctness.decision-quality: Org-level decisions are made with appropriate speed and rigor.
_distinctness.pressure: Workload is sustainable; burnout signals are visible and addressed.

dimensions.label: Organizational Clarity
dimensions.description: How clearly priorities, roles, and direction are communicated and understood across the org.

scoreBands.narrative: Clarity is the missing ingredient. People are working hard but on different priorities — and they're starting to feel it.
Some teams have line-of-sight; others are guessing. Clarity is leader-by-leader, not org-level.
Priorities are visible and shared. Most people can name what's most important this quarter without prompting.

dimensions.label: Accountability
dimensions.description: How reliably commitments are kept; how directly underperformance is addressed.

scoreBands.narrative: Commitments slide without consequence. Underperformers are accommodated, not addressed. High performers notice — and start to leave.
Accountability lives where individual managers create it. The org-level expectation isn't clear or consistent.
Commitments are taken seriously. Performance gaps get named — often kindly, always plainly.

dimensions.label: Talent Health
dimensions.description: Whether the right people are in the right roles; whether retention is intentional.

scoreBands.narrative: Wrong people in key seats. Retention is reactive — you find out someone's leaving when they tell you. Hiring is filling gaps, not building strength.
Talent is a mixed picture. A few critical roles are right; others are stretched or mismatched. Retention conversations happen, but late.
You know who your A-players are. They know they're A-players. Succession is something you can name, not just hope for.

dimensions.label: Decision Quality
dimensions.description: How well org-level decisions get made — speed, rigor, and willingness to revisit when wrong.

scoreBands.narrative: Decisions stall or get made by whoever pushes hardest. Reversing a bad call feels like losing face. You're paying for slow or poor decisions in dollars and morale.
Decisions get made — eventually. Quality varies with who's in the room. Hard calls get deferred more often than they should.
Decisions are made by the right people at the right altitude. Reversibility is understood. Speed and rigor are balanced — usually.
Pressure is constant and the team knows it. Burnout signals are visible. The org is running on people's reserves, not its systems.
Some teams have headroom; others are flat-out. Workload conversations happen at performance reviews, not before.
Pace is intentional. Capacity is named. Pressure spikes are visible and time-bound.

questions.text: Most people in our organization can name the top three priorities for this quarter without checking.
Roles and decision rights are clear enough that people rarely step on each other's work.
I regularly hear different leaders give contradictory direction on the same topic.
Our strategy is communicated in language that a new hire could understand by week two.
Important changes in direction often reach the team late — they hear it secondhand.
When someone commits to a deliverable, the rest of us assume it will land on time.
We have at least one chronic underperformer who's been protected from honest feedback for over a year.
Leaders here are willing to have hard performance conversations promptly, not just at annual review time.
Missed commitments are usually explained away rather than examined.
When something goes wrong, we focus on the upstream cause more than the downstream blame.
I can name our top three people whose departure would meaningfully damage the organization.
Our high-performers have had explicit conversations about their next role here.
We find out people are leaving when they resign, not before.
We have at least a rough succession picture for our most critical roles.
We've hired into a key role recently knowing we were settling for a B+ fit because the timeline pressed.
Most decisions get made by the people closest to the work, not pushed up to the most senior person available.
Important decisions routinely stall or get re-litigated for weeks.
When we realize a decision was wrong, we reverse it quickly without too much face-saving.
Decisions get made by whoever pushes hardest more often than by whoever has the best information.
We have a clear way to tell reversible from irreversible decisions, and we move faster on the former.
More than half the team is operating in a sustained state of overload.
We have honest conversations about capacity before piling on more work.
Burnout signs (irritability, sloppy work, withdrawal) are visible and not being addressed.
Pressure spikes here are time-bound — we know when the push ends.
Leaders model sustainable pace, including taking real time off.

totalBands.label: Pressure building
totalBands.narrative: Pressure is building. The org is showing signs of strain in multiple dimensions. Most people would tell you something has to give — but the conversation hasn't happened openly. Start with the dimension scoring lowest below; that's where the leverage is highest.

totalBands.label: Mixed signal
totalBands.narrative: Some parts of the organization are healthy; others are exposed. The risk is letting the exposed dimensions drag the healthy ones down. Pick the lowest-scoring dimension below and spend the next 30 days focused there.

totalBands.label: Healthy
totalBands.narrative: Most signals point healthy. The work now is protecting it — staying honest about emerging weak spots before they become structural problems.
